choiceReviews.rationale: Supported: aggregate-local ORDER BY Position processes the supplied positions in ascending order, and NULL ON NULL converts the middle SQL NULL into a JSON null element. Together they derive ["z",null,"a"]. Positions are distinct, so no unresolved ordering tie affects the result. This exact expression fits a positional export preserving missing-value slots; the conclusion uses the documented Azure SQL Database behavior, not SQL Server 2025 availability.

Contradicted: ascending Position supplies the right label order, but ABSENT ON NULL omits the SQL NULL element. The derived array is ["z","a"], with no middle placeholder. This unchanged expression fits a compact export that intentionally skips missing labels while retaining increasing position order. The source makes this omission policy the default when no null clause is supplied, reinforcing why explicit NULL ON NULL is needed here.

Contradicted: NULL ON NULL preserves the missing-label slot, but ORDER BY Position DESC places position 30 before 20 and 10. The derived array is ["a",null,"z"], not the requested sequence. This exact expression would be correct for a reverse-position export that preserves null placeholders. The source's aggregate ordering and null-clause contracts govern independent choices; preserving cardinality alone cannot satisfy the stated ordering requirement.

Contradicted: descending Position reverses the labels and ABSENT ON NULL removes the middle SQL NULL, yielding ["a","z"]. This identical expression is suitable for an export that deliberately requests descending positions and excludes missing labels. It is not invalid syntax merely because both choices oppose this contract. The documented ordering and null-omission rules explain the concrete alternative without relying on the physical order of the VALUES rows.
